headline: Buenos Aires Feb 2026 demonstrations were labor-reform protests, unrelated to gentrification or nomads
detail: Checked specifically for a gentrification/nomad-backlash pattern; the Feb 2026 demonstrations found are labor-reform related and do not indicate such a pattern.

headline: Marrakech shows real-estate-driven gentrification but no organized anti-nomad backlash
detail: Medina rents are climbing and riad buyouts continue, with foreigners making up 70-80% of luxury real-estate buyers; no organized backlash against remote workers found this pass — reads as ordinary background displacement rather than an emerging protest pattern.

headline: CDMX short-term-rental-cap enforcement reportedly paused for World Cup while evictions accelerate
detail: Previously logged nomad-targeting street marches are now linked to the World Cup; enforcement of the short-term-rental cap is reportedly paused until after the tournament while evictions continue to accelerate.

headline: Joint task force auditing foreign-owned businesses in Chiang Mai; some nationalities' visa-free stays cut to 30 days
detail: A 188-officer joint task force has been auditing foreign-owned hotels, businesses, and nominee-ownership structures through 2026, finding Hotel Act and Immigration Act violations and shell companies using Thai nominees to dodge ownership caps. Visa-run patterns are drawing rising scrutiny, and some nationalities have already had visa-free stays cut to 30 days.

headline: Oct 26, 2025 midterm legislative elections resolved in a stabilizing direction
detail: Milei's LLA won decisively, calming markets — logged as a closed, reassuring event rather than an open political-transition risk.

headline: Belize "crackdown" headline refers to internal ministry corruption, not foreign-business or nomad enforcement
detail: The one enforcement-sounding headline found for Belize concerns its own immigration ministry addressing internal corruption within its own department — unrelated to foreign businesses or nomads; worth naming since the headline alone could otherwise read as a false match.

headline: Visa rejection rates reportedly up 20-30%, tighter tax reporting on foreign platform income
detail: One trade-press source frames this as a "digital nomad visa crisis" affecting Medellin and Bogota, alongside tighter DIAN tax-reporting on foreign digital-platform income. Confidence Medium — not independently corroborated; a task was filed to confirm or downgrade.

headline: Law 5275/2026 closes the in-country tourist-to-Digital-Nomad-Visa conversion route
detail: A real tightening of the visa mechanism itself, not an enforcement campaign against people already resident — arriving on a tourist visa and converting to the Digital Nomad Visa from inside the country is no longer possible.

headline: New Digital Nomad category brings mandatory on-site inspections and broader document-request authority
detail: Regulatory tightening tied to the new Digital Nomad category includes mandatory on-site inspections, broader document-request authority, and sponsor-registration revocation — aimed at registration hygiene and employer-sponsored categories, not a targeted campaign against foreign-owned businesses.

headline: Judicial Reform Phase 2 continues Mexico's judiciary overhaul; rule-of-law concerns not yet reflected in red-flags
detail: The next judicial election (postponed from 2027 to 2028) continues an overhaul that already replaced nearly all federal and state judges by popular vote. Documented concerns include USMCA objections and organized-crime/political-elite influence risk on a less-professionalized judiciary. Not yet reflected in the country's own red-flags file; a task was filed to address it.

headline: New PSP enforcement unit (UNEF) sharply increases in-country immigration enforcement
detail: UNEF, under the PSP, is now fully operational and running in-country compliance inspections; one operation ("Miraculous Land") broke up a 4,000-migrant illegal-regularization ring. Notices-to-leave jumped from 444 (2024) to 23,134 (2025). Stated target is irregular/undocumented migration and smuggling, not nomad-visa holders, but D8 holders now sit inside a system doing far more in-country enforcement than before.

headline: Chega's continued rise marks an ongoing political-fragmentation trend not yet reflected in red-flags
detail: The Jan-Feb 2026 presidential election already resolved (Seguro/Socialist beat Chega's Ventura 67-33%), but Chega's continued rise — 23.5% first round, now the country's second-largest party across three parliamentary elections since 2022 — is a real ongoing trend analysts call "the collapse of centrism." Not reflected in the country's own red-flags file; a task was filed to address it.

headline: Phuket rolling out its own tourist-tax and immigration-crackdown measures
detail: Part of a Southeast Asia-wide tourism-cluster trend (alongside Bali, Boracay, Penang, and Langkawi) of new tourist-tax and immigration-enforcement measures in 2026; the pattern has not yet reached this project's Latin American, European, African, or US candidates.

headline: Short-term-rental crackdown escalating; homestay permits up roughly 400%
detail: Domestic zoning enforcement, not tied to foreign ownership or visa status — a different axis from the Southeast Asia-style nomad-enforcement pattern, but a real and escalating local factor.

headline: Short-term-rental crackdown escalating; homestay permits up roughly 400%
detail: Domestic zoning enforcement, not tied to foreign ownership or visa status — a different axis from the Southeast Asia-style nomad-enforcement pattern, but a real and escalating local factor.

headline: Nov 3, 2026 midterms feature contested House control amid confidence-undermining concerns
detail: Documented concern that some tactics (mid-decade redistricting, prosecution of political opponents) are "meant to undermine confidence" in the process, plus active foreign disinformation targeting the election. Logged as background — reads as a domestic-institutional-trust question rather than a location-specific one; no task filed.

headline: Belize's general Permanent Residency page was repeatedly cited for a 14-day-a-year cap on time spent outside the country; that figure couldn't be confirmed anywhere on the actual page, and has been dropped
detail: A 14-day cumulative-absence limit was stated, in several places across this site's Belize material, as part of this route's residency requirement. Repeated, independently worded checks of the government page cited for it found no such day-count language anywhere on it — only a requirement that the arrival stamp be at least one year old at the time of application, plus a discretionary 'financially stable' standard with no fixed figure. The 14-day figure has been removed everywhere it appeared, rather than left standing without a real source.

headline: Guatemala's presidential approval rating and impeachment-related figures didn't match their cited source, and have been corrected
detail: An approval percentage and counts of impeachment petitions and immunity-removal attempts against the president, previously shown as sourced facts, did not actually appear anywhere in the article cited for them. Replaced with what that article does say: the president won more than 60% of the vote in the 2023 election, and roughly 93% of criminal cases under the outgoing chief prosecutor's office remain unaddressed.

headline: A Puerto Vallarta safety entry understated a named cartel figure's actual rank, and separately relied on shakier sourcing for a reward figure and family-relationship detail about him; both are now corrected to match reliable reporting.
detail: The entry previously described this figure only as a local leader in the Puerto Vallarta area. A direct re-read of the article cited for that finding shows a bigger claim: US authorities rank him tied for the group's national second-in-command. Separately, the reward figure and the family-relationship detail attached to him are real, but weren't sourced well enough — one citation for them couldn't be verified and was dropped, and the family-relationship detail had been misread from a passage in the same article that's actually about a different named individual. Both are now correctly sourced elsewhere. This doesn't change the site's safety score for Puerto Vallarta — the underlying risk was already reflected in that score.

headline: A decree number cited as separate legal backing for part of Paraguay's Rentista visa explanation didn't appear on the page cited for it, and has been removed from that citation; whether the decree itself is real remains an open question.
detail: A specific decree, presented as its own legal basis for one of the Rentista visa's income benchmarks, doesn't appear anywhere on the page originally cited for it — checked twice, independently. It has been removed from that citation and replaced with the law the same page actually confirms as the route's real governing law, Law 6984/2022. The same decree number does turn up, independently, on a different page this site also cites for the same benchmark — so this isn't a closed case of a fabricated decree; it's an open one, not yet resolved either way. The benchmark figure itself is unaffected regardless — it was already, and still is, correctly described as a multiple of Paraguay's minimum wage.

headline: South Africa's Remote Work Visa duration and renewal terms were stated incorrectly, and have been corrected to match the actual immigration law
detail: The visa was previously described as an initial 12-month grant, renewable annually up to 3 years total. The document cited for that structure doesn't actually say it. The real mechanism, read directly from South Africa's own immigration law: a single grant, for a period the immigration department decides, capped at 3 years — not a fixed 12-month term with automatic renewal. Whether or how it can be renewed past that single grant is still genuinely unconfirmed anywhere official. This doesn't change how the site evaluates outcomes on this route, but it changes what a reader should actually expect the visa to look like.

headline: A currency-handling gap meant certain foreign-currency figures were silently read as US dollars; Buenos Aires's own cost comparison was one of the affected rows, and it has been corrected
detail: When a monthly cost or income figure used a currency symbol the site's comparison tool didn't yet recognise, the figure was read as if it were already in US dollars rather than being flagged as unconvertible. For Buenos Aires, this meant a peso figure of roughly 2 million a month was compared as if it were about two million dollars. The tool now recognises a much wider set of currency symbols and, for any it still can't convert, says so rather than guessing.

headline: Spain's non-lucrative visa income bar was being evaluated at roughly a twelfth of its real value; corrected on the site
detail: A parsing gap in how the site reads a monthly income figure written next to its own annual equivalent caused the monthly bar to be divided by twelve a second time. Spain's non-lucrative visa threshold was being compared at roughly $216 a month instead of its real value, about $2,592 a month — the same gap also touched Spain's digital-nomad visa and Costa Rica's digital-nomad visa. Anyone who checked this route before 27 August 2026 should re-check their own numbers against the corrected figure.

headline: Argentina's midterm legislative elections were dated a year too late — they were held on 26 October 2025, not 2026 — and the date has been corrected
detail: An entry published on 7 July 2026 described Argentina's midterm legislative elections as already resolved, while dating them to 26 October 2026 — a date that had not yet arrived. The election was real; the year was wrong. Argentina's convocation decree, Decreto 335/2025, published in the Boletín Oficial on 20 May 2025, calls voters to elect national senators and deputies on 26 October 2025, and the government's own legal-text mirror of the same decree carries identical wording — so the election had already happened when that entry was written. The wrong year originated in an early summary that cited no source, and was then repeated across several places on this site without being checked against the decree. Only the year has been corrected: the description of the election's outcome, and Argentina's political-stability rating, are unchanged.

headline: A Belize healthcare red flag overstated its source — "no oncology or endocrinology capacity nationally" has been corrected to what the cited source actually says
detail: A Belize red-flag entry stated that specialty care for oncology and endocrinology was unavailable nationally, an absolute claim. The cited source, expatsi.com's Belize healthcare report, does not name either specialty — it describes the health system nationally as having limited capacity for complex conditions such as cancer and heart disease. The oncology/endocrinology wording was an unconfirmed specificity upgrade beyond what the source supports. The identical over-claim, drawn from the same source, was already found and corrected on a related fact about distance to emergency and specialist care on 2026-08-25; this second instance of the same wording was missed at the time and continued to ship unchanged until now. The wording has been brought in line with what the source actually says; the underlying picture — that complex specialty care is not available domestically and requires travel, mainly to Mexico — is unchanged.

headline: We labelled two Corozal purchase-price figures "more than one source, cross-checked". We cannot show that any source carries them. The labels are corrected.
detail: Two Corozal purchase-price figures — an entry/fixer tier of $90,000-$100,000 and a realistic 2-3 bedroom range of $150,000-$220,000 — carried the label "more than one source, cross-checked". They should not have. On 25 August we re-checked. The page we cited is a cost-of-living guide for a different part of Belize and gives no Corozal purchase prices. The page we most likely meant to cite, on the same site, does not carry either figure; its own Corozal examples start at $235,000, above both ranges. The two other sites we named as cross-checks were never retrieved. We cannot currently show any source that carries either number. Both figures now carry the "one source" label — that one source is our own research, not a listing we can point to — and are marked speculative. The figures themselves are unchanged and nothing else on the site moves. Our citation failed, not the figures. They stay until we've sourced them properly. If you are weighing a Corozal purchase against them, treat them as an unconfirmed starting point, not a checked range.

headline: Ten Guatemala facts and four visa routes carried sourcing labels stronger than what we can actually show. The underlying data mostly checked out; the labels didn't.
detail:
Ten fact rows in Guatemala's data claimed a sourcing tier stronger than a direct re-check could support -- most labelled "more than one source, cross-checked" when the real picture was thinner. The nationality lists themselves held up well: 35 entries spot-checked across the Category B and C lists against a source we retrieved to check them, zero mismatches, plus five of Category A's confirmed against the immigration authority's own published examples. What moved is the citation, not the data.

Three of the ten claims -- the Digital Nomad visa rejecting passive income, the same route rejecting pension income, and a claim that Salvadoran/Honduran/Nicaraguan nationals move into Guatemala on national ID with no day cap -- have NO source, at any tier, that actually states them. They were this project's own inferences, carried as sourced findings. A fourth, related but genuinely different case: the claim that San Pedro La Laguna sits inside Lake Atitlan's 200-metre lakeshore reserve band rests on exactly ONE source, a real-estate blog -- not nothing, but the government agency that actually administers that band is reachable, was read directly, and never names the town or states a band width. These are not the same problem and are not interchangeable: one is an unsupported claim, the other is a real but single-sourced one.

Five further rows -- Guatemala's AML/beneficial-ownership reform taking force, the 2026 judicial-appointment reset, and the Category A/B/C nationality lists' own full enumeration -- were labelled "more than one source, cross-checked" on the strength of press reporting, law-firm commentary, and Wikipedia agreeing with each other. None of those source types can sustain that label here: press, law-firm commentary, and Wikipedia record as a single lower tier regardless of how many of them agree, because none is a primary institutional document. A tenth row (inter-town hiking-trail robbery risk) sits closer to the unsupported end: its only named source has never actually been fetched -- two separate attempts to reach it have both failed.

The same nationality-list claims also live in a second table -- the one describing entry routes rather than individual facts -- and four rows there move as well: Guatemala's three visa categories (visa-exempt, consular visa, consulted visa) and the CA-4 free-movement arrangement with El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. All four had been labelled "more than one source, cross-checked". Three now record what they actually rest on, a single aggregator page, while holding the same middle confidence. The CA-4 row drops furthest: nothing but an encyclopaedia entry stands behind it, no institutional source states it, and it is now marked at the weakest tier this project uses. The lists these routes describe are the same ones that spot-checked clean above -- what changes is the routes' sourcing labels, not their content.

Nothing about the underlying facts changes -- the AML law is still entering force, the visa-exempt lists are still accurate on spot-check, San Pedro is still, most likely, inside the band. What changes is that the sourcing labels now say how well each claim can actually be checked, not how well it reads.

headline: We dated a Guatemala Constitutional Court appointment and a Comptroller-commission swearing-in from the day their news coverage published, not the day they happened. Both are fixed, one day off each.
detail:
A Guatemala fact row stated Congress reappointed Constitutional Court magistrate Roberto Molina Barreto on 2026-03-07, and that the Comptroller General's nominating commission was installed by 2026-08-12. Both dates were wrong by one day, from two related but distinct errors: the first read a news article's publish date as the date of the event it reports; the second carried a scheduled date forward as though it had been confirmed.

The Constitutional Court date was sourced to a Tico Times article published 2026-03-07 -- but the article's own text says Molina Barreto "was selected Friday," and 2026-03-06 is the Friday; 2026-03-07 is a Saturday. Prensa Libre, timestamped 2026-03-06 03:33h, reports the vote count directly and is the real source for the date: 2026-03-06. The Comptroller-commission date had a related but distinct problem -- "installed by 2026-08-12" was a scheduled date, carried forward as though it had been confirmed to happen on schedule. Infobae's 2026-08-13 report of the actual swearing-in is the real date.

Both dates are now corrected everywhere they appeared. The wrong Constitutional Court date had actually been recorded twice in the same entry -- once as the date itself and once repeated in the explanation of where that date came from -- and both instances are fixed, not just the first. A related, previously-open sourcing note on the same row (the Attorney General's name and start date, resting on three Wikipedia pages rather than a press source) is also closed out: a direct press citation for that pairing has been found and is now cited.

The sharpest fact here is the mechanism, not the one-day gap: the article cited for an event's date says the event happened the day before the article was published. That is worth watching for elsewhere -- a publish date is not an event date, and a scheduled date is not a confirmed one.

headline: We showed a lake-warming rate as Lake Atitlán's water-quality reading. The source we cited does not contain that number, and we have removed the entry.
detail:
Our Lake Atitlán entry headed "Lake cyanobacteria/water-quality problem" gave, as its value, a warming rate: +0.34 °C per decade. We got two things wrong, and the second one we had already spotted ourselves.

We cited NASA's Earth Observatory page on the harmful algae bloom in Lake Atitlán. We have now retrieved that page and searched its bytes directly. The figure is not on it — not "0.34", not "warming", not "temperature", not "decade", nowhere. The page does describe the cyanobacteria bloom, and does name untreated sewage, agriculture and deforestation among its causes, so it supports what we say about the blooms themselves. It simply never carried the number we hung on it. Our own source list for the lake's water quality names two further sources, a research paper and a magazine article, and we have never retrieved either. So there is no source we can point to that carries this figure.

The second problem is that it was the wrong kind of answer. A warming rate is a possible cause of algae blooms; it is not a measure of whether the water is safe to swim in. Our own review of this site on 10 July 2026 said exactly that about this exact entry — that it reduced the water-quality problem to a warming number and dropped the health-relevant content. Nobody acted on it, and the number stayed on the page from that day until now.

We have removed the figure from the page and struck the claim from the research note behind it. We are not saying the figure is false. We are saying we cannot show a source for it, and that it was answering the wrong question. What stays is the substance: the recurring toxic-algae blooms, the untreated sewage, agricultural runoff and deforestation-driven erosion behind them, the presence of E. coli and Giardia, and the joint NASA/USAID bloom-forecasting dashboard that monitors the lake. Lake Atitlán's nature-and-water score is unchanged at 3 — the reasoning behind that score always rested on the blooms and the sewage, never on the warming figure. This was the only fact we had filed under nature and water-adjacency for Lake Atitlán, so that heading now shows no facts on file for the location. That is accurate, and we would rather show nothing there than a number we cannot stand behind.

headline: Thirteen Guatemala cost-of-living figures showed the date we wrote them down, not the date the figure was true. No price has changed — only the dates beside them.
detail:
Every price and budget figure on this site carries a date. The date on a fact is when the figure was true or the rule took effect. Where we have re-checked it, the check date is shown too. On thirteen Guatemala cost-of-living entries the date shown was the day we typed the entry in — a check date sitting in the field that says when the figure was true.

Ten are Antigua entries — four rent bands for the historic centre plus one rate someone reports actually paying, two restaurant-meal tiers, a single-person monthly budget, one resident's own lived monthly spend, and a couple's short-stay ledger. Three are around Lake Atitlán: a Panajachel café-coffee band, a Panajachel restaurant main-dish band, and a two-bedroom rent band for San Pedro La Laguna.

Nine of the thirteen now show the date their own source carries, and in most cases that is older than what we had been displaying: six of the Antigua rent and budget figures come from pages last updated in April 2025, and three rent bands are dated to March 2026, which is the month their publishers say their figures describe. Where a source gives both a vintage for its figures and a later date on which the page itself was edited, the vintage is the one that belongs beside the number, and that is the choice made here. The remaining four are the more uncomfortable part: their sources carry no date at all — two are merchants' own posted menus, two are guide pages with no publication line — so those entries now say plainly that no date is stated, with the day we checked them shown beside that, instead of a date we had supplied ourselves.

The part worth being blunt about is that fixing this required no research. Every correct date was already written into our own note on the same entry, by the same person who entered it, on the same day. We had made this a rule for ourselves back in July — a figure's date does not move just because we looked again — and then broke it. This is a failure to record something we already knew, not a failure to find it out.

This is not the same as the two Guatemala date corrections published on 6 September, and it should not be read as correcting them twice. Those were two specific one-day errors inside individual facts — a court reappointment and a swearing-in — where the event's own date was wrong. Here nothing about any fact's content is wrong and no figure has moved; what was wrong is the date stamp shown beside each figure, which is what tells a reader how old a price is.

We are not claiming the problem is finished. A mechanical test for the same defect flags about forty further entries across ten countries as possibly carrying it — some of those will turn out to be legitimate, because a figure's real date genuinely can be the day it was read. And that test can only see entries that carry a record of having been checked, so an entry with the same problem and no such record is invisible to it. The true size of this is not known. What is fixed today is these thirteen, and three more in Marrakech corrected alongside them.

headline: Three Marrakech cost figures showed the date we wrote them down, not the date the figure was true. No price has changed — only the dates beside them.
detail:
Every price figure on this site carries a date. The date on a fact is when the figure was true or the rule took effect. Where we have re-checked it, the check date is shown too. Three Marrakech entries instead showed the day we typed them in — a check date sitting in the field that says when the figure was true.

Two are rent figures from an Arabic-language Marrakech daily: the ceiling on what landlords charge local families for an unfurnished flat, and the level economic-housing rents reached after the September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake. Both now show their articles' own publication dates, August 2025 and September 2023. The second of those matters more than it looks: a rent level reported within weeks of the earthquake is a snapshot of that moment, and the date beside it is the only thing telling you it is not a current reading. The third entry is a coffee price taken from one restaurant's posted menu, and a posted menu carries no date — so it now says plainly that no date is stated, with the day we checked it shown beside that, rather than a date we had supplied ourselves.

No price has changed. Only the dates did, and they now say what they were always meant to say.

Fixing this required no research. Every correct date was already written into our own note on the same entry, by the same person who entered it, on the same day. We had made this a rule for ourselves back in July — a figure's date does not move just because we looked again — and then broke it. This is a failure to record something we already knew, not a failure to find it out.

The same check found the same problem on thirteen Guatemala entries, corrected alongside these; they are one review, not two separate mistakes. It is not a closed set either. A mechanical test flags about forty further entries across ten countries as possibly carrying the same defect, some of which will prove legitimate, and it is blind to any entry that carries no record of having been checked. What is fixed today is these sixteen.

headline: Four Argentine income-type refusals withdrawn: the answer for retirees and remote workers moves from "no" to "we don't know yet".
detail:
Four claims about Argentine residency routes are withdrawn: that the Pensionado route rejects investment income and rejects remote work income, that the Rentista route rejects remote work income, and that the Digital Nomad route rejects investment income.

Three of the four cite Argentina's own government service pages, which is the strongest kind of source there is -- but citing a government site is not the same as having read the page that states the rule, and we had not. The fourth rests on a commercial visa-guide site.

These rows all said the same kind of thing: that a particular visa route will not accept a particular kind of income -- a pension, investment income, or money earned working remotely for clients abroad. That is a hard "no" to a reader, and a hard no is exactly the sort of claim that stops someone applying for a route they might actually qualify for.

When we went back to check where each of these refusals came from, we could not show it. In every case the citation points at a website rather than at a page we have actually retrieved and read saying so. That does not make the claims wrong. Several of them are probably right. It means we cannot demonstrate them, and we are not willing to leave a hard no standing on a source we have not opened.

So these rows are held rather than deleted. They render nothing and count for nothing until someone opens the source page and confirms what it says. If it turns out to say what we claimed, the row comes straight back unchanged.

What a reader sees change: for two of the eight reader profiles the Argentina answer moves off a confirmed refusal and onto "not enough information". Nothing about Argentina got better or worse. We stopped saying no with a confidence we could not back.

headline: Two Belize retirement-programme income refusals withdrawn; the Belize answer for remote workers moves from "no" to "unclear".
detail:
Two claims about Belize's Qualified Retirement Programme are withdrawn: that it rejects income earned working remotely for foreign clients, and that it rejects income earned working locally in Belize.

Both cite the Belize Tourism Board's own retirement-programme page. That is the right source to have used. We had not retrieved it to confirm it says this.

What a reader sees change: for one of the eight reader profiles, Belize moves off a confirmed refusal and onto an unresolved one. The programme's income threshold and its other conditions are unaffected.

headline: Two Malaysian De Rantau income-type refusals withdrawn. No verdict on the board changes.

What a reader sees change: no verdict on this board moves. Of all the countries in this batch, this is the one most likely to be resolved quickly, because the document that would settle it is published and reachable.

headline: Three Portuguese income-type refusals withdrawn -- the largest effect of any country here: fourteen verdicts move.
detail:
Three claims about Portuguese residency routes are withdrawn: that the D7 visa rejects income earned working remotely, and that the D8 visa rejects investment income and rejects pension income.

All three rest on commercial visa-guide and golden-visa marketing sites rather than on anything published by the Portuguese authorities. Portugal's D7 and D8 are among the most written-about routes in this whole dataset, which is part of the problem: there is a great deal of secondary commentary and we leaned on it.

These rows all said the same kind of thing: that a particular visa route will not accept a particular kind of income -- a pension, investment income, or money earned working remotely for clients abroad. That is a hard "no" to a reader, and a hard no is exactly the sort of claim that stops someone applying for a route they might actually qualify for.

When we went back to check where each of these refusals came from, we could not show it. In every case the citation points at a website rather than at a page we have actually retrieved and read saying so. That does not make the claims wrong. Several of them are probably right. It means we cannot demonstrate them, and we are not willing to leave a hard no standing on a source we have not opened.

So these rows are held rather than deleted. They render nothing and count for nothing until someone opens the source page and confirms what it says. If it turns out to say what we claimed, the row comes straight back unchanged.

What a reader sees change: more here than anywhere else in this batch -- fourteen verdicts move across Lisbon, Porto, Lagos and the country view. For one profile a confirmed refusal becomes an unresolved one. For another, the refusal stands, but on the income amount rather than the income type -- the route is still out of reach, for a different and better-supported reason. For two more profiles a conditional yes becomes an explicit "undetermined on income type", which is a less comfortable answer and a more honest one.

headline: Thirteen Thai Long-Term Resident income refusals withdrawn -- the largest single withdrawal here. No verdict on the board changes.
detail:
Thirteen claims about Thailand's Long-Term Resident visa are withdrawn, covering all four LTR categories -- Wealthy Global Citizen, Wealthy Pensioner, Work-from-Thailand Professional and Highly Skilled Professional -- and the reduced-threshold variants of several of them. Each said that a given category refuses pension, investment, or remote work income.

All thirteen cite the same thing: the front door of the official LTR website, not any page within it. A site's homepage cannot state thirteen specific rules, so thirteen specific claims cannot rest on it. This is the clearest case in the batch.

These rows all said the same kind of thing: that a particular visa route will not accept a particular kind of income -- a pension, investment income, or money earned working remotely for clients abroad. That is a hard "no" to a reader, and a hard no is exactly the sort of claim that stops someone applying for a route they might actually qualify for.

When we went back to check where each of these refusals came from, we could not show it. In every case the citation points at a website rather than at a page we have actually retrieved and read saying so. That does not make the claims wrong. Several of them are probably right. It means we cannot demonstrate them, and we are not willing to leave a hard no standing on a source we have not opened.

So these rows are held rather than deleted. They render nothing and count for nothing until someone opens the source page and confirms what it says. If it turns out to say what we claimed, the row comes straight back unchanged.

What a reader sees change: no verdict on this board moves, because the profiles that reach these routes are decided on other grounds. What does change is the routes themselves -- across the four LTR categories, thirteen income-type cells stop saying "rejected" and start saying "undetermined". Access to the official LTR site has since been arranged, so this is a batch we expect to resolve rather than one we expect to sit on.

headline: New Antigua rent and budget research widened the documented cost range, and one profile's verdict moves off "clears comfortably".
detail:
Antigua's documented monthly cost range was $500-$800. It is now $300-$1500.

Nothing got more expensive. The old range rested on a single figure -- a furnished one-bedroom in the historic centre. September research added more: a general one-bedroom estimate for the centre starting lower, and a single-person all-in monthly budget reaching higher. The range is wider because we now know more about the spread, not because prices moved.

What a reader sees change: for one of the eight reader profiles, Antigua moves from clearing the cost bar with room to spare, to sitting inside the range rather than above it. That is the honest reading of a wider evidence base. It is also the only verdict anywhere in this update that moves to a harder answer.

Worth being plain about why this is appearing now: the underlying research was published on this site earlier, but the verdicts were not recalculated at the same time. They have been now. For a period the site showed cost figures and a verdict that no longer matched them.

headline: Chiang Mai's cost range now rests on one-bedroom rents rather than two-bedroom, and one profile's verdict improves.
detail:
Chiang Mai's documented monthly cost range was $386-$2230. It is now $208-$624.

The old range was built from a two-bedroom rental spread, which was the only rent evidence we had. September research added one-bedroom figures, including a rent a resident actually pays. For a single person those are the right rows to use, and they are both lower and much narrower than the two-bedroom spread.

What a reader sees change: for one of the eight reader profiles, Chiang Mai moves from an uncertain answer to a clear one. The city did not get cheaper; we stopped describing a single person's costs with a two-bedroom range.

This also settles a comparison that was wrong on the site. Chiang Mai now reads as cheaper than Bangkok, which every cross-checked figure we hold supports. Separately, a Bangkok budget figure that contradicted its own supporting note and every neighbouring city has been withdrawn pending a read of its source; Bangkok's range is unchanged, because that figure was never what set it.

headline: We told you Antigua's department had 3 homicides per 100,000. Guatemala's statistics institute says 15.4 -- we were wrong by five times, in the reassuring direction.
detail:
Until today this site reported a homicide rate of 3 per 100,000 for Sacatepéquez, the department Antigua sits in, and cited a guide site that credits "MININT homicide data · INE" -- Guatemala's National Institute of Statistics.

We went to INE's own publication. Its Perfil Estadístico Sacatepéquez gives the department's homicide rate for 2023 as 15.4 per 100,000, under its own chart heading "Tasa por cada 100,000 habitantes", with the five-year series running 14.6, 5.4, 10.3, 12.4, 15.4 from 2019 to 2023. A second table in the same document counts 63 homicide victims in the department that year, which is what 15.4 per 100,000 produces. The two agree with each other and neither agrees with us.

The figure on this page is now 15.4, dated 2023 -- the year the number describes -- and sourced to INE directly.

Two things worth saying plainly. The error ran in the direction that makes a place look safer, which is the worse direction for anyone weighing it. And the source we used credited a government body for a number that body contradicts -- so the problem was never that we used a secondary source, it was that we never opened the primary one it named.

headline: Two Taghazout rent figures are withdrawn -- the page we cited for them never said them.
detail:
Two rent figures for Taghazout are withdrawn: 4,000-5,000 dirhams a month for a two-bedroom in Tamraght, and 8,000-10,000 for an ocean-view two-bedroom.

We cited a single page for both. That page's domain is now parked -- it serves a placeholder, not an article -- so we went to the web archive for what it said when we used it. There are two captures. Neither contains either figure. Neither mentions Tamraght, neither gives a price in dirhams, neither mentions ocean-view units. The page's actual cost table is in US dollars and covers a one-bedroom.

So this is not a dead link. The figures were attributed to a page that never carried them, and the archive shows that was already true on the day we cited it.

We could not replace them. Every source that prices Taghazout rents monthly is one we have no access to, and the nearest usable anchor covers Agadir rather than Taghazout -- close enough to make the withdrawn figures look plausible, which is exactly why we are not substituting it. Looking right is not the same as being sourced.

Taghazout's remaining cost figures come from a cost-of-living aggregator, and are now labelled as such.

headline: Two Thai rent ranges are withdrawn: the site we cited was quoting Moroccan dirhams on its Thailand pages.
detail:
Two rent figures are withdrawn -- Bangkok's 11,000-140,000 baht a month for a two-bedroom, and Phuket's 14,000-160,000.

Both came from one property portal. When we re-read the pages it serves today, its prices are in Moroccan dirhams, not Thai baht -- the currency appears 185 times on the Bangkok page against two appearances of the baht symbol. The only baht figures in the page's own text describe studios, not two-bedrooms, and none of them matches what we published.

Property sites change; we cannot tell whether the page gave baht when we first used it. What we can say is that the page does not support these figures now, so they do not stand.

Bangkok is the larger consequence. Withdrawing that row leaves the city with one monthly cost figure: Thailand's National Statistical Office household-expenditure survey, 32,736 baht a month per household. A household is not one person. So Bangkok's cost check now reads "The cost figures on file here describe a household, not one person -- not assessed for a single reader" rather than giving a range that was never about a single reader.

Three verdicts move. Two improve: one profile's answers for both Bangkok and Phuket go from "Near-miss" to "Clears". One gets harder -- a different profile's Phuket answer moves to "Doesn't clear". All three move because we withdrew figures, not because anything about either city changed.

The harder answer rests on a band whose floor is Phuket's own household figure -- 38,941 baht a month per household, from the same survey -- which is the mismatch this correction is about; we have not yet fixed it everywhere it occurs.

Separately, Phuket's cost cross-check is relabelled. It was recorded as confirmed by more than one source; both of those sources are cost-of-living aggregators, and two aggregators agreeing is not confirmation. It still stands, as a single aggregator figure.

Bangkok, Phuket and Taghazout are removed from the rent comparison chart until they have a figure to plot.
